This Loneliness Awareness Week, Radhika Sanghani shares how she realised that she was one of the 74 per cent of young adults who often feel lonely – and why stepping out of her comfort zone helped her to make friends for life

Removed from bookmarks

Are you lonely? If you are, can you admit it out loud?

When I was at my loneliest, I couldn’t. The thought of simply saying “I’m lonely” felt impossibly mortifying. I was in my late twenties – I was meant to be at my peak, living a life that older generations envied. Instead, I was the one who was jealous of my parents’ friends and their fulfilling social lives.

Back then, I was at a crossroads. I no longer had much in common with my childhood friends who were settling into marriage and motherhood, and the more time I spent around them – a group who were, incidentally, all very close to each other – the lonelier I felt. I had plenty of single acquaintances at work, but few of them had transitioned into close friends. And even though I had a diary full of weekday drinks and dinners, they didn’t give me the connection I was so deeply craving. Often, I’d get home feeling lonelier than before I’d left the house.

It turns out, ironically, that I’m not alone in my struggle. Young people aged between 16 and 34 are suffering more loneliness than those over 55, with 73.8 per cent saying they often feel lonely or feel lonely every day, according to the Opinion Exchange. Four in 10 living alone said they felt lonely, but 31 per cent who lived with housemates also felt lonely, as did 25 per cent of those who lived with family.

That is aligned with my experience: I could feel lonely both living alone and when I was living with housemates. The problem was not being surrounded by people – it was how connected (or disconnected) I felt to them. And unfortunately, connection was the one thing lacking from my social life.

Simone Heng, author of Let’s Talk About Loneliness, explains that the definition of loneliness is the gap between “the kind and amount of connection you desire and the kind and amount of connection you’re getting”. The problem with talking about this out loud to the people you’re not getting that connection from is that they could take it badly and lead to social disconnection – the exact opposite of what you need.

“Then there’s social stigma behind loneliness,” she adds. “We’ve all watched true crime shows and know these delinquent people in society seem to come from the fringes and are lonely and socially rejected. We don’t want to be lumped into that. We fear that by saying we’re lonely, we’re pushing ourselves closer to that definition of being on the fringes.”

These associations around loneliness persist, and it’s why it took me such a long time to admit my loneliness to myself. I hated the thought of labelling myself as lonely – it felt embarrassing; weak. Olivia Laing, author of The Lonely City, recently wrote: “Even the lonely have a tendency to believe that loneliness is their own fault, a product of something essentially dislikable in their own being.”

I finally managed to accept my loneliness on a Saturday night. I was home alone, feeling like a Bridget Jones cliche as I watched movies with pizza in my pyjamas, when I realised I couldn’t deny it any more: I was lonely. As embarrassing as it was, I needed to stop pretending things were fine and accept that I felt sad and lonely.

Looking back, that night was crucial in fixing my loneliness problem. Because, as I sobbed to myself about the state of my friendships (not to mention my love life), I let myself feel my feelings. I stopped running from the pain and shame, or trying to numb myself by making more plans and scrolling through socials; I finally allowed myself to grieve.

Heng says this moment of “self-connection” is incredibly important: “Most people who are lonely don’t know it, unless they’ve had a breakup or have lost a loved one. You have to have a strong relationship with yourself to identify loneliness, because the lonely brain isn’t rational – it can trick you into misidentifying what you’re going through. The barrier to having that realisation can also come from the fact that we’re so busy, so there’s a lack of sitting with ourselves to actually feel loneliness. You need to put your phone down and check in with yourself to recognise if you’re lonely.”

This could be why loneliness levels are so much higher among young people who are chronically lonely – but also chronically online. There’s even a new trend of “loneliness influencers”, people like @lanasololife, a 24-year-old solo influencer posting reels like, “You’re a single girl who lives alone and has no friends, so you go grocery shopping at 10.04pm”.

I forced myself to be vulnerable by courageously hovering around at the end of yoga classes to speak to others, and then eventually suggesting coffee

“The commodification of vulnerability for views is something we need to watch out for,” warns Heng of these influencers. “One of the markers of lonely people is oversharing. The brain feels starved of connection, so it thinks, ‘I’ll tell them my life story’. If you don’t have another person to do that to, you have the internet and TikTok.”

My shame stopped me from ever admitting my loneliness online, but after that night of self-connection, things shifted. I’d been so focused on external connection that I’d forgotten about my relationship with myself. Simply accepting where I was allowed me to begin to connect more to myself. I knew it would take time to make new friends, so in the meantime, my focus needed to be on spending time with myself.

Cheryl Rickman, author of Navigating Loneliness: How to Connect with Yourself and Others, stresses just how important that is: “Use time alone to build self-awareness and get to know and like yourself. Inner connection creates a foundation for better outer connection, too. Because the better we feel in our own company, the better we become at being in others’ company.”

Before I ventured out in search of new company, I did something Heng and Rickham both recommend: I started volunteering. I created a nail bar at my local Age UK centre, giving manicures to elderly ladies who were often far lonelier than I. It helped me to see things outside of my own perspective and allowed me to create connections with people I would otherwise never have met. When I went through a devastating breakup, these women comforted me with their life experience, reminding me how much bigger life was than just one man.

It also helped me move past the belief that making friends as an adult was impossible. So, slowly, I began my mission. I’d just started freelancing for a big media company filled with people my age, so instead of popping out for a solo sandwich, I suggested lunch with my coworkers. But that wasn’t enough to turn our connection from acquaintances to friends; I had to suggest plans outside of work. Like going to watch a play on a Thursday evening, and, when I felt brave enough, a Saturday brunch.

“I still remember thinking it was weird when you invited me to an event and I barely knew you,” one of my closest friends tells me now, eight years on. “But I’m so glad you did.” It turned out that being “weird” and doing the very un-London thing of reaching out to strangers was necessary when it came to making real friends. As professor and researcher Brene Brown says, it’s only when you show vulnerability that you can make true connections.

I forced myself to be vulnerable by courageously hovering around at the end of yoga classes to speak to others, and then eventually suggesting coffee. That was terrifying enough, but then on our coffee dates, I had to show up as the real me and open up – without going too far and scaring them away by oversharing.

Not all those friendships have lasted into my mid-thirties – but a surprising amount have, and I still treasure each and every one for being there when I needed it

It didn’t always work and lead to real friendship, but the times it did gave me the confidence to keep on going. I realised that more often than not, I was met with just as much vulnerability as I offered. I stopped fearing awkward exchanges with strangers – instead I found myself with weekend plans to stay in the Cotswolds with a friend of a friend I’d sat next to at a wedding, and spending Christmas in the Grand Canyon with two American women I’d met on a rock climbing course.

“Take out noise-cancelling headphones when you’re in the city,” says Heng when it comes to her top tips for breaking free of loneliness. “That blocks opportunities for connection. If you can, be of service. And join groups where you have commonality: if you’re doing an activity you enjoy like running or paint and sip, it helps to bridge the lulls in awkward conversations and provides you with a common interest to talk about what’s right in front of you.”

For me, it wasn’t just one thing that helped heal my loneliness. It was the combination of learning to sit in my feelings, enjoy my own company, being of service and eventually making new friends I truly had things in common with that brought me the connection I was craving.

Not all those friendships have lasted into my mid-thirties – but a surprising amount have, and I still treasure each and every one for being there when I needed it. Even the ones that faded away taught me that it is possible to create new friendships at any point in life, which means I’m no longer scared of feeling lonely ever again. I don’t have to cling onto friends or relationships to meet my needs – I can always find new ones, and most importantly, I can be a friend to myself.
